analysis.one_liner: Exempts hydraulic fracturing for oil and gas production from federal underground-injection drinking water rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on April 18, 2005 and received no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Safe Drinking Water Act, pumping fluids deep underground counts as 'underground injection' and is regulated to protect drinking water. This bill would have rewritten that definition to say that fluids and propping agents pumped underground during hydraulic fracturing ('fracking') for oil and gas are not underground injection at all, removing them from those federal safeguards. It also would have excluded underground natural gas storage from the definition. The bill died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers: fracturing would no longer fall under federal underground-injection permitting under the Safe Drinking Water Act, removing a federal regulatory hook over the fluids pumped into wells during fracking. Underground natural gas storage operators would likewise be excluded from the definition.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Safe Drinking Water Act's definition of 'underground injection' so that the injection of fluids or propping agents during hydraulic fracturing operations related to oil or gas production is excluded from the term [S2][S3].
It also excludes the underground injection of natural gas for storage from the definition, shielding gas storage wells from the same rules [S3].

By shrinking the definition of underground injection, the bill would remove fracturing operations from the federal permitting framework Congress wrote to safeguard underground sources of drinking water [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who drink water drawn from aquifers near fracturing operations would bear any added risk, since fracturing fluids would no longer be covered by the Safe Drinking Water Act's underground-injection safeguards. Communities near fracking sites would depend instead on state-level rules, which vary.

drawbacks.text: Excluding fracturing from 'underground injection' would leave the fluids pumped into wells for fracking outside the federal drinking-water protection program, so communities near drilling would rely on state rules of uneven strength [S2][S3].

The bill would remove a federal backstop without creating any substitute national standard, so the level of protection would depend on where a well is drilled rather than a single national floor [S2].

Supporters would argue the existing definition was never meant to cover fracturing and that regulation through a drinking-water permitting program adds cost without matching risk; that cost, they would say, falls on domestic energy production.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs one way: it relieves oil and gas producers of federal permitting obligations under the Safe Drinking Water Act. The cost is borne diffusely by anyone whose drinking water sits above or near fracturing activity, who would lose a federal safeguard and would have to rely on state rules. There is no compensating public benefit in the bill itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, so it died quietly at the end of the Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Inhofe introduced the bill on April 18, 2005 [S1][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works — its only action of the Congress [S5].
The committee never reported the bill and the full Senate never voted on it; its action history ends with the referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because this bill died, drinking-water safeguards in the Safe Drinking Water Act were left intact by this vehicle. Notably, Congress enacted essentially the same fracking exemption later that year as part of the Energy Policy Act of 2005, so the underlying policy relief for producers did become law through another route.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers, via the 2005 energy bill

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-OK); chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt hydraulic fracturing from the Safe Drinking Water Act's underground-injection definition; as committee chair he held the power to move it but never advanced it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no recorded opposition and no recorded support beyond its sponsor: zero cosponsors, no committee action, and no floor vote, so no partisan split is visible in the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have removed hydraulic fracturing for oil and gas production from the Safe Drinking Water Act's underground-injection rules, cutting producers' federal permitting obligations while shifting any groundwater risk to people living near wells [S2][S3].

The bill also excludes natural gas storage injection from the definition, removing those wells from the same federal permitting framework; storage wells are generally less associated with drinking-water contamination than fracturing, so the public stakes here are smaller [S3].
